description: Test your knowledge of Principles of Genetics, Chromosomal Aberrations & Clinical Genetics.

cards.text: What is triploidy and what is the most common cause?
cards.answer: Triploidy (3n, 69 chromosomes) is nearly always lethal, aborting in the first trimester. The most common cause (66%) is dispermy—fertilization of a normal ovum by two sperm.

tip.tip: Three sets = triple trouble; remember 66% from dispermy

cards.text: What is the key difference between diandric and digynic triploidy?
cards.answer: Diandric triploidy (extra paternal set) produces a partial hydatidiform mole with a large placenta. Digynic triploidy (extra maternal set) produces severe asymmetric growth restriction with a small placenta.

tip.tip: Diandric = Dad's extra = big placenta; Digynic = Mom's extra = small baby

cards.text: Define non-disjunction and explain how it leads to trisomy.
cards.answer: Non-disjunction is failure of chromosomes to separate during meiosis, producing gametes with n+1 or n-1 chromosomes. Fertilization of an n+1 gamete with a normal n gamete produces trisomy (2n+1).

tip.tip: Non-dis = no separation = unequal chromosome distribution

cards.answer: Reciprocal translocation is mutual exchange between two chromosomes; carriers form a quadrivalent during meiosis producing unbalanced gametes. Robertsonian translocation is fusion of acrocentric chromosomes with loss of short arms containing redundant rRNA genes; carriers have 45 chromosomes but are phenotypically normal.

tip.tip: Reciprocal = swap; Robertsonian = acrocentric fusion (5 chromosomes only)

cards.text: Why is rob(14;21) the most clinically important Robertsonian translocation?
cards.answer: Carriers of rob(14;21) can produce offspring with translocation Down syndrome. Female carriers have 10-15% empirical risk and male carriers 1-2% risk of an affected child.

tip.tip: rob(14;21) = how young parents can have Down syndrome offspring

cards.text: What is the most common Robertsonian translocation and its frequency?
cards.answer: rob(13;14) is the most common Robertsonian translocation, occurring in approximately 1 in 1,300 individuals.

tip.tip: 13&14 together = most frequent variation in the population

cards.text: Which chromosomes can undergo Robertsonian translocation and why?
cards.answer: Only the five acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22) can undergo Robertsonian translocation because they can fuse at their centromeres with loss of short arms containing only redundant ribosomal RNA genes.
Aneuploidy is gain or loss of individual chromosomes (e.g., trisomy 2n+1 or monosomy 2n-1). Euploidy is gain or loss of complete chromosome sets (e.g., triploidy 3n or tetraploidy 4n).

tip.tip: Aneuploid = odd one out; Euploid = complete extra set
